strengths: Lane: subjective, fit to the user. It meets D1 and the rule against lazy launches exactly. Every browser starts in `start()`. `#warm` is the only code that creates a browser, and it runs at start or after a fault's release, never inside a call. `#forward` only leases a slot that is already warm.
Setup has one code place (`#warm`, composed by `start()`) and so does teardown (`#release`, composed by `destroy()`). The fault path reuses `#release`. This is the D8 shape the user asked for.

Every slot launches at once, which meets D8's 'as early and as eagerly as possible'. The handshake waits only for the first warm browser, so a spare never adds to onset. M1 and M2 measure what concurrent warm-up costs instead of assuming it (D5).
A spare is a full slot: process, profile, isolated context, page, and toolset. Failover therefore builds nothing (D3, and D7's 'warm before work that needs it arrives').

It checks liveness before each hand-out. A `ping` runs before every call. It is triggered by work, never by a schedule, so D7's 'knows which browsers are alive and answering before it hands one work' holds for every call. The cost is one added member on `Browser`.

It has the smallest surface of the three: `endpoint` and `ping` on `Browser`, one option, one variable, and three error codes. There is no public pool class, no change to `src/core`, and no release dependency on `@orkestrel/mcp`.
Exit, socket loss, hang, and a crash of the current page all take one recovery path: replace the slot.
The D3 plan is concrete. It runs on the target Windows host, reports every run, and defaults to 0 spares until the user rules.

Attacked and held: delaying `transport.start()` holds back every handshake path. `StdioServerTransport.start()` is the only place that attaches the `data` listener (mcp src/server/transports/StdioServerTransport.ts:83-100).
defects: It declines the D9 hook the user named. Leaving stdin unread has three costs. A `ping` sent before `initialize` goes unanswered, though clients.md:7 lets a client send one. A paused stdin with no `data` listener never emits `end`, so a client that gives up during setup goes unseen. The failure reaches the client only as exit 1 plus stderr. Right: take the library proposal's U1 hook (grafts).

D8 has a gap after the server is killed. The sweep removes dead owners' profiles but leaves their detached POSIX Chromium processes running (Risks, 'POSIX orphans'; src/server/helpers.ts:368-371 spawns with `detached` everywhere except Windows). Right: attach to the recorded endpoint and close it (grafts).

The D6 ceiling can break. In unit 2, `#warm` awaits `after` with 'its rejection ignored'. `Browser.#terminate` throws 'Browser process did not exit after SIGKILL' (src/server/Browser.ts:1139-1141), so a replacement can launch beside a process that survived. Right: re-warm only after a release confirmed the browser was destroyed; otherwise keep the profile and retire the slot.

After an idle loss, `#admit` refuses the next call only to deliver the notice (ruling 3). That costs the agent a call its `navigate` would have used. Right: run the call and open its result with a one-time note, as the library proposal does.
The `spares` option (0 to 2) counts browsers beside the session's, but the user states the pool's size (D6: 'configured size', 'two, three at most'). `BROWSE_SPARES=1` means two browsers.

`BrowserSlot` is exported from `src/server/types.ts` although it is an internal record with no consumer (its own Tension). Keep it out of the public surface by whatever parity mechanism the Orchestrator picks.
The sweep removes bare `UUID` profiles, which a live server of an older version on the same root might own (its own Tension; question to the user).
At the default of 0 spares, the call after a loss waits for a launch already in progress (failure table, 'waits for the re-warm'). That is acceptable only as the D3 baseline that M3 measures.
With one session holder, D6's 'balances work across them' reduces to failover. Every proposal shares this; it is a question to the user.

Referred to the objective lane, not ruled. First: two concurrent first calls both enter `#admit` while `#lease` is undefined and both await `#wait`. Whether they receive the same slot depends on microtask order. Second: a replacement context restarts its reference counter at 0 (src/core/BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-349), so after recovery an old `eN` reference can select a new element. The analyst found the second.

strengths: It takes D9 the way the user framed it. A `handshake` hook in `@orkestrel/mcp` 0.0.36 gates legacy `initialize` and `server/discover`, and a `ping` is answered meanwhile. An `MCPError` rejection is answered under the request id. The release order is stated: U1 publishes before U2 re-pins.
When setup fails, it answers `initialize` with the error, keeps answering until stdin ends, and then exits 1. Nothing races the write, so no write-completion API is needed.

At the next start it reclaims a killed server's Chromium: it attaches to the recorded endpoint and closes that browser, using the existing `BrowserInterface.close()` (src/server/types.ts:296-304). The GUID in the endpoint path keeps a reused port from matching. This meets D8's 'including after a crash'.
`acquire` never launches. `BROWSE_POOL` takes 1 to 3, states the user's D6 count directly, and enforces 3 as the ceiling.
After an idle loss, the next result opens with a one-time note on a call that runs. A call in flight during the loss fails with the loss text.
It repairs the 9222 probe for launches on port 0. Eager start would otherwise turn a debugging Chrome on 9222 into a refusal at every server start.
defects: Its public `BrowserPool` surface goes far beyond 'small and simple'. It adds a class, a factory, a status union, a member snapshot, `member(id)` and `members()`, holder strings, a FIFO waiter queue, rotation, eight events, seven error codes, four constants, two helpers, and endpoint files. Its own Tension 11 concedes that `member(id)` works against the minimal API. Browse is the only real consumer.

Setup and teardown are each split across layers, against D8's one place for each. Setup: the pool launches browsers, `BrowserMCPServer.start()` builds the session, and browse rebuilds the session after a loss or a renderer crash. Teardown: `pool.destroy`, `lease.release` (which closes contexts), browse `destroy` (the toolset), and the start sweep.

A spare is warm only at the browser level. The context, page, and toolset are built after promotion, so failover pays for a session build (D7: 'each browser is warm before work that needs it arrives').

Launches run one at a time: member 1 starts after member 0 is ready. That is less eager than D8's 'as early and as eagerly as possible'. It rejects concurrent warm-up on a claim it never measured (D5).

Hang detection adds a `timeout` event to `CDPClient` in `src/core`, a re-emit on `Browser`, and a check in the pool, while another writer edits `src/core`. A `ping` before each call covers the same D7 need with one member.
It refuses with -32603, which the package documents as a fault code that carries no detail (mcp src/core/constants.ts:285-295).

strengths: It states the limits honestly. Without a poll, D7 cannot mean continuous proof that an idle browser answers. No cleanup can run synchronously after an uncatchable kill (D8).
It never exceeds configured capacity while a failed process drains, and it keeps the profile when termination is unconfirmed. The server proposal needs exactly this fix.

It names two real seams. The tool layer passes only the message, so an error code is lost on the wire. A replacement context restarts the per-context reference counter (src/core/BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-349).
It refuses with -32000, the JSON-RPC implementation-defined server error, plus a stable code in `data`. It also refuses to replay an interrupted action automatically.
Its measurement plan compares the lazy server, an eager single browser, and an eager pool. It reports distributions and fixes no threshold in advance (D5).
defects: It is the heaviest design, against 'small and simple'. It has eight phases, generations, lease ids, three deadlines, recovery credits, and a durable ownership protocol (an exclusive reclamation claim, symlink and reparse-point checks, process identity beyond a PID). It adds a reference allocator in `src/core` and four mechanisms in `@orkestrel/mcp` (an initialization callback, per-connection state, write-completion observation, and a closure signal), where one hook serves stdio browse.

Its replacement credit allows 'a replacement attempt per configured slot during an owner lifetime', and neither readiness nor calls replenish it. The session's browser therefore retires on its second crash in a long session, which fails D2.

It gates `initialize` on every configured slot and treats a spare that fails to start as a startup failure. Onset then carries the slowest of the concurrent launches against Codex's 10 s default (clients.md:19), and one transient spare failure fails the whole server.
A call that arrives during recovery is refused at once and does not wait. With one browser, the agent retries blind until the replacement is ready.
It exits after the error response, which needs a write-completion API. The library proposal stays up until stdin ends and needs no new API.
Like the library proposal, it makes the pool a public library class with no second consumer.
Its units are a table with no file ownership, roles, or run commands per unit. It calls its type sketch 'contract direction, not checked declarations'.

grafts: From the library proposal (U1, Q1), the `@orkestrel/mcp` `handshake` hook. It replaces ruling 1's unread stdin and turns conditional unit 7 into the first unit. Browse sets `#starting` first in `start()`, then starts the transport and attaches the `end`, SIGINT, and SIGTERM listeners. It passes `createMCPServer` a `handshake` handler that returns `#starting`. The handshake still waits for the first warm browser only, as the server proposal rules. When setup fails, every slot is already released through `#release`. The transport keeps answering `initialize` and every later request with the refusal until stdin ends. Then `destroy()` runs and the bin exits 1. The server never exits before the answer.

From the analyst (section 1), the refusal code. The hook rejects with `new MCPError(message, -32000, { code: 'BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE' })`, and the message carries the cause. Use `JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR` (mcp src/core/constants.ts:297-305), not -32603, which the package keeps for faults that carry no detail, and not -32602.

From the library proposal (Q3, 'Profiles a killed server left behind', and U5 (f)), reclaiming orphans by endpoint. After `connect()`, `#warm` writes that life's endpoint to a file inside the life's own `PID-UUID` profile directory. For each profile whose owner is dead, the `start()` sweep calls `createBrowser({ cdp: { endpoint } })`, then `connect()` and `close()`, and only then removes the directory. Keep the server proposal's `PID-UUID` naming and keep the sweep as the only place that reclaims. Add no sibling `.endpoint` file.

From the analyst (the races table and the cleanup row 'Cleanup cannot confirm termination'), the capacity rule. A slot re-warms only after its `#release` resolved with the browser destroyed. When `browser.destroy()` rejects, `#release` keeps the profile, retires the slot, and records the failure for `destroy()`'s aggregate. This replaces unit 2's `#warm` step 'awaits `after` (its rejection ignored)'.

From the library proposal (Q3, 'How the agent learns', and U6 (e) and (f)), the loss notice. After an idle loss, the next call runs and its result opens with a one-time note naming the last address and what was lost. A call in flight still fails with the loss text. From the analyst (section 3): each text carries the `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH` code token, because the tool layer passes only the message (map.md:32).

From the library proposal (Q5, 'The 9222 fix', and U3 (e)), the probe fix. `Browser.connect()` with `discover: false` probes `cdp.port` only when the caller set `cdp.port`, because a launch on port 0 reads its endpoint from its own child and cannot attach to another browser. Update the `BrowserCDPOptions` remarks (src/server/types.ts:101-106) and land the change in server unit 1.

From the library proposal (Q5), naming the setting by size. Use `pool: { size }` from 1 through 3 with `BROWSE_POOL`, defaulting to 1 until the user's D3 ruling, in place of `spares` (0 to 2) and `BROWSE_SPARES`. The setting then states the count the user gave in D6 and enforces 3 as the validated ceiling.
verdict.pool:
Lane: subjective, fit to the user. Ruling: keep the pool in the browser package, private to `BrowserMCPServer`, as the server proposal's slot array. Do not use `@orkestrel/pool` as it is, do not improve it for this case, and add no public `BrowserPool`.

Reasons: `@orkestrel/pool`'s semantics differ at the points D7 names.
(1) It creates inside `acquire` whenever nothing is idle and capacity remains (C:\Users\mikes\WebstormProjects\pool\src\core\Pool.ts:272-276). After a dead browser is disposed, the session's next call would therefore launch a browser on a caller's demand, which D7 forbids.
(2) `release()` returns a record to idle without validating it (Pool.ts:470-483), and validation runs only at handoff (Pool.ts:293-305). Nothing observes a leased or idle browser, but D7 asks for liveness at all times.
(3) There is no warm floor (scaffold guides/pool.md:7), so D3's warm spare would need an acquire-everything-then-release-everything workaround at start.
(4) `PoolToken` and `PoolEventMap` carry no holder (pool src/core/types.ts:35-58), but D7 asks the lease to say who holds each browser.
(5) It cannot evict one idle record. `clear()` disposes every idle record (Pool.ts:147-159), so replacing one dead spare would also destroy the healthy one.

Improving the package would add four features (a warm floor, a mode that never creates on acquire, per-record eviction, and a holder) to a generic engine whose guide states it has no warm floor. All of that would serve a fixed array of 1 to 3 slots, where the ceiling already holds by construction: each slot holds one incarnation, and its replacement starts only after a confirmed release. The package also pins `@orkestrel/contract` ^0.0.18 beside the browser's ^0.0.19, which installs a second copy of the contract package.

Record this semantic difference in the design record as the proof `.claude/rules/quality.md` § Ecosystem reuse requires, citing capabilities.md §2-3 and the Pool.ts lines in the preceding reasons. No public `BrowserPool` (the library and analyst proposals) because the only consumer in this change is browse. Its first test consumer is the deferred shared-browser change, which can extract the slot logic then.
verdict.mcp:
Ruling: change `@orkestrel/mcp` with one hook and nothing else. Add `MCPServerOptions.handshake?: MCPHandshakeHandler`, where `MCPHandshakeHandler = (options: MCPMethodOptions) => Promise<void>`. Expose it as `MCPServerInterface.handshake`, which `createMCPLegacy` reads the same way it reads `identity`.

1. Legacy `initialize` (mcp src/core/MCPLegacy.ts:140-150) and modern `server/discover` await the hook before they build their result.
2. `ping` (MCPLegacy.ts:151-152) never awaits it.
3. An `MCPError` rejection is answered under the request id as `{ code: error.code, message: error.message, data: error.context }`.
4. Any other rejection is answered with -32603 and no detail, and emits `error` exactly once, following the package's convention (src/core/constants.ts:285-295).
5. The hook receives the per-request signal. `bindServer` aborts that signal when the request is cancelled or the transport closes (src/core/helpers.ts:1874-1877, 1908-1912), and then writes nothing (helpers.ts:1888).
6. With no hook, every existing answer is unchanged.

No per-connection state, write-completion API, closure signal, or `logging` capability is added: a stdio browse awaits one setup promise per process and stays up until stdin ends. `buildInitializeResult` keeps `{ tools: {} }`.

Attacked and held: a parked `initialize` does not block a later `ping`. `StdioServerTransport` hands each line synchronously to the async listener in `bindServer`, which is never awaited per message (StdioServerTransport.ts:136-140, helpers.ts:1868-1907).

Specification text it conforms to, from the MCP 2025-11-25 lifecycle page as recorded in clients.md:
- The client sends `initialize` first and 'SHOULD NOT send requests other than pings before the server has responded' (clients.md:7). Pings can therefore arrive while `initialize` is parked, which is why `ping` is never gated.
- An error reply to `initialize` is allowed; the page's example is -32602 (clients.md:9). Refusing a failed setup with an error response is therefore conformant.
- Implementations set timeouts on every request and cancel on expiry (clients.md:11). The hook's wait ends on the request's signal.
- Sending `notifications/message` requires declaring `logging` (clients.md:12). The hook sends nothing and declares nothing.

Browse refuses with -32000, the JSON-RPC 2.0 range reserved for implementation-defined server errors (-32000 to -32099, documented at constants.ts:297-305), with `data.code` set to `BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`.

Release order: the user publishes `@orkestrel/mcp` 0.0.36 from their terminal. The browser then re-pins `^0.0.36` (a caret on 0.0.x pins the patch), updates the lockfile, and refreshes `guides/mcp.md` (the library proposal's U2) before any browse unit that uses the hook.
questions: D6 says the pool 'balances work across them', but with one stdio session every proposal reduces the second browser to failover. Is failover what you meant? Or must browse serve a second holder at once, for example parallel agents sharing one browse server, or a replay running beside interactive work? A second holder changes the lease from one session to several.

D7 asks for liveness 'at all times', and AGENTS.md § Design laws forbids polling. Do you accept events plus a check before every call, where a hang in an idle spare is found only when the spare is handed work? Or do you allow a scheduled check of idle spares as an exception to the polling law?

Does `initialize` wait for the first warm browser or for every configured one? Waiting for the first means onset carries the fastest launch and a broken spare is retired while the session runs on fewer. Waiting for every one means a broken spare fails at onset (D4), but onset carries the slowest launch against Codex's 10 s default.

May the first start of the new version delete `ROOT/.profiles/<uuid>` directories that carry no owner pid? A live server of an older version on the same root might own them. Otherwise they stay until you remove them by hand.

strengths: Each incarnation is released once. `#fault` returns early unless `#slots[index]?.browser === browser` and the slot is in `#ready` (proposal-server.md:382-388), so an exit, a socket drop, and a page crash on one incarnation trigger one release. Its own teardown raises no fault, which holds against the code: Browser.ts:389 ignores an exit after destroy, and Browser.ts:1144-1158 emits `destroy`, never `disconnect`.

A replacement launches only after its predecessor's release settles (`after`, proposal-server.md:345, 387), so the pool never runs more Chromium than its size. Unit 3 asserts that each `connect()` starts after the predecessor's `destroy()` settled (proposal-server.md:407).

A call during recovery parks on `#change`, which is an event and not a poll, and runs on a spare or on the re-warm. With every slot retired, the call answers `BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE` with the cause (proposal-server.md:234, 354, 268).

The crash-loop bound is reasoned from the case: a deterministic cause recurs, and a transient one clears on one retry. A leased fault is paced by the agent and visible to it (proposal-server.md:68-71).
The renderer-crash filter holds against the code: `toolset.view` returns `#page ?? #view` (BrowserToolset.ts:360-362, 537-539), and a page's `url` stays readable after death (BrowserFrame.ts:84-85).
After destroy, the cleanup proofs check pids (`ESRCH`), endpoint ports, profiles, the SIGINT and SIGTERM listener counts, and the input `end` listener (proposal-server.md:367-372).
defects: proposal-server.md:29-32, 517: stdin stays unread until a browser is warm. The lifecycle lets a client ping before the `initialize` answer (clients.md:7), and that ping waits for the launch, against the ping utility's prompt-reply requirement, which proposal-server.md:517 itself names. An end of stdin during setup also goes unseen until a browser is warm (proposal-server.md:533). Right: start the transport at once (mcp server factories.ts:493-495) and gate `initialize` through an `@orkestrel/mcp` hook.

proposal-server.md:33, 258: a failed start shows only as exit 1 and a stderr line, with no answer and no in-protocol cause. How a client displays an exit before `initialize` is unread (clients.md:28). Right: answer `initialize` with a coded JSON-RPC error that carries the cause.

proposal-server.md:259, 523: the 9222 false refusal stays. `browse` launches on port 0 (helpers.ts:363), yet `#assertPortFree` probes 9222 (Browser.ts:320-322, 543-549). With an eager start, a developer's Chrome on 9222 now fails every session start, and the strike retry repeats a deterministic refusal. Right: skip the occupancy probe when `cdp.port` is unset and keep it for an explicit port. The probe's documented purpose (types.ts:101-106) cannot apply to a port-0 launch.

proposal-server.md:393-394, with 384-385 and 355: `#admit` grants the lease, then pings. A hung spare is therefore faulted as a leased slot. The agent gets a session-loss notice naming the spare's `about:blank`, no strike is counted, and the next lease grant resets the strikes. A spare that warms and then hangs costs one command deadline per call with no bound. Right: check before leasing, count a failed hand-out check as an unleased fault that strikes, and then try the next ready slot.

proposal-server.md:353, 267: `#release` destroys the toolset, then the browser. On an owned browser, `Browser.destroy()` awaits a CDP `context.close()` for each context before `#terminate` (Browser.ts:848-856, 951-958; BrowserContext.ts:365-379). A hung browser's release therefore waits through successive command deadlines, and the `after`-gated re-warm waits with it, as does the next call when there are no spares. The failure-table row says only 'fault, same as an exit'. Right: on a fault, end the incarnation's process before any CDP teardown, or bound the whole release.
proposal-server.md:50, 267: `ping` sends `Browser.getVersion`, which the browser process answers, so a hung renderer passes it. The failure table has no row for a renderer that stops answering.

proposal-server.md:57-66: recovery builds a fresh context, and its reference counter restarts at 0 (BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-350). A reference the agent took before the crash can then select a different element after recovery. The proposal does not address this.

proposal-server.md:530, 72-76: after a SIGKILL on POSIX, the detached Chromium keeps running (helpers.ts:368-371), and the start sweep deletes that live orphan's profile. D8 requires that nothing is left behind. The sweep also removes bare `UUID` profiles that a live older server may own (proposal-server.md:73, 526).

proposal-server.md:217-218: `BROWSER_SERVER_PROFILE_PATTERN` duplicates `parseBrowserLockEntry` (helpers.ts:59-65) with a looser pattern (`\d+` admits pid 0 and leading zeros). Reuse the helper with `formatBrowserLockEntry` (helpers.ts:47-49).

proposal-server.md:342 vs 271: on a signal during setup, unit 2 rethrows `BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`, while the failure table says `BROWSER_TOOLSET_ENDED`. Either way, a SIGTERM ends the process with exit 1 and an error line (main.ts:30-34).

strengths: The handshake hook conforms to the specification, and its key claim holds: `bindServer` dispatches each message without awaiting it (mcp core/helpers.ts:1868; mcp server/factories.ts:115-118), so a ping is answered while `initialize` is parked. U1 (a) to (f) prove the ping, the error mapping, the unchanged default, `server/discover`, and the abort on close.

It does not exit on its own after the error. Unbinding aborts in-flight requests, and an aborted request's answer is never written (mcp helpers.ts:1888, 1913-1919), so the proposal correctly keeps answering until input ends (proposal-library.md:36, 343).
The transport reads from the start, so an end of stdin or a signal during setup reaches `destroy()` at once. A `destroy()` during setup resolves `start()` (proposal-library.md:37, 329).
It fixes the 9222 false refusal for port-0 launches and keeps the refusal for an explicit port, with a service proof (proposal-library.md:110; U3 e).
It checks before leasing: an idle member that misses its hand-out check counts as a failed life, and the next ready member is tried (proposal-library.md:70, 320).

It reclaims the Chromium a killed server left behind. Each life records its endpoint; the next start attaches and sends `Browser.close` before `rm`, and the browser GUID in the endpoint path rejects a reused port (proposal-library.md:76-80; U5 f).

A renderer crash rebuilds the session on the same browser instead of killing Chromium (proposal-library.md:323). Serial launches keep the onset path to one uncontended member (proposal-library.md:49, 100).
defects: proposal-library.md:319, 63: the hung-browser row ends 'then as for an exit', which destroys the browser. On an owned browser, `Browser.destroy()` closes each context over CDP before `#terminate` (Browser.ts:848-856, 951-958), so recovery waits through successive command deadlines. U4 f and U5 c assert only that the pid ends. Right: on a fault, terminate the process before any CDP teardown, or bound the whole release, and assert the replacement `launch` event within one command deadline of the fault.

proposal-library.md:57, 319: the challenge is `version()` under the browser's own timeout. Detection therefore spans two command deadlines, calls admitted meanwhile hang as well, and a hung renderer passes because `Browser.getVersion` is answered by the browser process. Right: stop admission during the challenge, also challenge the page's session, take the deadline from M4 (proposal-library.md:418), and add a renderer-hang row.
proposal-library.md:62-66: the rebuilt context restarts its reference counter at 0 (BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-350), so a stale reference can act on a different element after a loss.

proposal-library.md:304, 314: at onset, the first launch failure retires member 0 with no retry, although Q3 reasons that one failure can be transient (proposal-library.md:73). A launch timeout under load then fails the session start.

proposal-library.md:77-79, 326: the endpoint record is written after the launch reads stderr. A kill between spawn and that write leaves an orphan the sweep cannot close. A recorded endpoint that does not answer still has its directory removed while the process may live. Right: remove a directory only after its browser is confirmed gone; otherwise keep it and report.

proposal-library.md:34: `-32603` for a setup failure is the code `MCPServer.#contain` gives every unexpected throw (MCPServer.ts:1775-1777), so the two cannot be told apart by code. Use `JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR` (-32000, constants.ts:305) with `data.code`.

proposal-library.md:10, 426: gating `server/discover` leaves a modern `tools/call` ungated, because modern requests bypass MCPLegacy (MCPLegacy.ts:90-92). Browse's execution path must await the same setup promise.

proposal-library.md:63, 317: the proposal has no rule for a termination that cannot be confirmed. `#terminate` throws after SIGKILL (Browser.ts:1139-1141), and the member then relaunches beside a surviving process.

strengths: It has the most complete race table: a call during recovery, a call queued before a crash, overlapping exit, socket, and renderer signals, a replacement that crashes before publication, a late attempt after shutdown, a stale release, a crash during teardown, a signal or end of stdin during launch, and the initialize-response race (proposal-analyst.md:123-134).
It uses generation identity: a fault invalidates its generation synchronously before async cleanup, and a late result never publishes (proposal-analyst.md:91, 127-131).

It catches defects the other two proposals miss, each verified against the code: references reused after a context rebuild (BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-350), the browser-versus-renderer challenge (proposal-analyst.md:79-81), teardown bounded as a whole against sequential CDP deadlines (proposal-analyst.md:311; Browser.ts:848-856), and an error code that the tool boundary drops (proposal-analyst.md:115).
It states the limits of D7 and D8 plainly: no continuous liveness proof exists without a poll, and no in-process cleanup can run after an uncatchable kill (proposal-analyst.md:5-6).

When termination cannot be confirmed, it keeps the ownership record and never relaunches past capacity (proposal-analyst.md:293, 348). It fixes the 9222 refusal and preserves the explicit-port check (proposal-analyst.md:279), and it uses an implementation-defined error code for a setup failure (proposal-analyst.md:37).
defects: proposal-analyst.md:22-24: `initialize` waits for every configured slot, and a spare that fails to start fails the whole startup. Concurrent launches on the weak hosts D6 names put the slowest launch on the onset path, against Codex's 10 s default (clients.md:19).

proposal-analyst.md:117: each slot gets one replacement credit per owner lifetime. With one browser, the second crash of a long session retires it until the user reconnects, but D2 asks `browse` to recover a crashed browser.

proposal-analyst.md:125, 144: a call during recovery is refused at once and never waits. With one browser, every call fails until the replacement is warm, and the agent gets no signal of when to retry.

proposal-analyst.md:30-34, 37: it adds mcp surface beyond the need. Per-connection initialization state is not required: the lifecycle constrains the client before `initialized` (clients.md:7-8) and does not require the server to refuse requests. The write-completion observation and closure signal exist only because `browse` would exit on its own; keeping the session open until input ends needs neither.

proposal-analyst.md:192-200: an eight-phase stored union (`idle`, `checking`, `stopping`, and `stopped` among them) works against D6's 'small and simple' and against the derive-state law. `BrowserPoolOptions` also requires three caller-supplied deadlines and an attempt count.
proposal-analyst.md:313-326: process identity 'stronger than a bare PID' has no native Node source. The mechanism is left open, and the fallback reports the failure instead of cleaning up.
proposal-analyst.md:273, 418-431: the type sketch is marked unchecked, and the units carry no owned files and no per-unit run commands.

grafts: From analyst § Cleanup ownership ('Bound teardown as a whole', proposal-analyst.md:311): on a fault, the member's process ends before any CDP teardown, or the whole release runs under one bound. Reason: `Browser.destroy()` on an owned browser awaits `#closeContexts` CDP calls before `#terminate` (Browser.ts:848-856, 951-958). Acceptance: with a SIGSTOPped browser, the replacement `launch` event arrives within one command deadline of the fault.

From analyst § 2 (proposal-analyst.md:79-81): on a CDP deadline, stop admitting work to the member, then challenge the affected page's session as well as `version()`. A page that misses the challenge takes the library's renderer-crash rebuild path. Add a 'renderer stops answering' row to the failure table, and take the challenge deadline from M4.

From analyst § 3 (proposal-analyst.md:113): a reference allocator owned by the session that never reuses a reference spelling within one MCP connection. Reason: each context's counter starts at 0 (BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-350). Acceptance: a reference taken before a kill does not resolve after recovery.

From analyst's race table (proposal-analyst.md:127) and server's `#fault` guard (proposal-server.md:382): each life has one invalidation and one cleanup promise. Listeners are keyed to the current `Browser` instance, and an event from a superseded instance is ignored. Acceptance: an overlapping process exit and socket close produce exactly one `crash` and one `launch`.

From analyst's failure table ('Cleanup cannot confirm termination', proposal-analyst.md:348): when `#terminate` throws after SIGKILL (Browser.ts:1139-1141), the pool keeps the profile and the endpoint record and retires the member rather than relaunching beside a surviving process.

From analyst § 3 (proposal-analyst.md:119): classify each launch failure. A missing executable, `ENOENT`, or an explicit-port refusal retires the member at once. A launch-deadline failure at onset gets one retry within `BROWSER_POOL_FAILURES`, replacing the library's retire-on-first-failure at onset (proposal-library.md:304, 314).

From analyst § Cleanup ('Remove only verified pool-owned paths after process release', proposal-analyst.md:295, 313): the start sweep removes a dead owner's directory only after its recorded browser is closed and confirmed gone, and keeps it otherwise. The pool directory exists before the first spawn, so a profile with no endpoint record is still found. Reading Chromium's own `DevToolsActivePort` file in that profile as a fallback is a candidate that is NOT-EVIDENCED in the portfolio; the sweep proof must establish it before use.

From server unit 2 acceptance (proposal-server.md:367-372): after `destroy()`, assert that every recorded endpoint port refuses connections and that the input `end` and `close` listener counts and the SIGINT and SIGTERM counts are back to baseline. Today the library's U6 (j) asserts only the signal counts.

From analyst § 1 (proposal-analyst.md:35, 37): browse rejects its handshake with `JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR` (-32000) and `data: { code }`, not -32603, and gates its modern `tools/call` path on the same setup promise, because modern requests bypass MCPLegacy (MCPLegacy.ts:90-92).
verdict.pool:
Lane: objective, judged under the correctness lens. Ruling: keep the pool in the browser package; do not use `@orkestrel/pool`, as it is or improved. The reasons follow.

- Pool.ts:272-276 creates a record only inside `#pump` for a queued waiter. After a crash, the replacement browser would therefore launch inside a caller's `acquire`, which breaks D3 ('no call pays a startup') and D7 ('never by a caller's demand').
- `validate` runs only at hand-out (Pool.ts:293-305, 356-409), and `release` recycles a record with no check (Pool.ts:470-483). Nothing observes a leased record, so a browser that dies while leased stays leased until its holder releases it.
- No method disposes one chosen record: `clear()` disposes the whole idle snapshot (Pool.ts:147-160), and `destroy()` ends the pool.
- `PoolEventMap` payloads are empty and `PoolToken` carries no holder (types.ts:35-58), so D7's 'tracked and known' and its holder record are absent.
- Improving the package would mean a warm floor that calls `create` outside `acquire`, contradicting its documented lazy contract (types.ts:64-66), plus eviction of a leased record and a failure bound to stop a floor from relaunching in a loop. Those are the supervisor semantics the user excluded, added to a generic engine that `@orkestrel/worker` depends on. It would also install `@orkestrel/contract` ^0.0.18 beside the browser's ^0.0.19.
- Splitting liveness between Pool's validate and dispose and the browser's event listeners creates cross-layer races, for example an exit event arriving while the record sits in `#validating` (Pool.ts:36, 293-305). One state machine in one class is provable.

For two or three browsers, the browser-side code is smaller than the pool change. Whether that class is the public `BrowserPool` in `src/server` or private to the server is referred to the subjective lane. Under correctness, the `src/server` class is preferred, because U4 proves each race against a real `Browser` over the fake process without the MCP layer. The default pool size is the user's D3 ruling.
verdict.mcp:
Ruling: change `@orkestrel/mcp` with one optional hook. Add nothing else: no logging, no per-connection state, and no write-completion API.

The shape:
- Add `handshake?: (options: MCPMethodOptions) => Promise<void>` to `MCPServerOptions`, expose it read-only on `MCPServerInterface`, and have `createMCPLegacy` pass it the way it passes `identity` (mcp core/factories.ts:88-90).
- `MCPLegacy` `case 'initialize'` (MCPLegacy.ts:140-150) awaits the hook under the request's signal before it builds the result. `case 'ping'` (MCPLegacy.ts:151-152) never awaits it. Because `bindServer` dispatches each message without awaiting it (mcp core/helpers.ts:1868; server/factories.ts:115-118), a ping is answered while `initialize` waits.
- `MCPServer` gates `server/discover` the same way.
- A rejection carrying an `MCPError` answers that code, message, and data under the request id. Any other rejection answers the fixed -32603 and emits one `error`, as `#contain` does (MCPServer.ts:1775-1777). Without a hook, every reply is unchanged.

Browse's side:
- Browse passes the setup promise that `start()` already began.
- On a setup failure it rejects with `JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR` (-32000, constants.ts:305) and `data: { code }`, then answers each later request with the same failure until input ends, and only then destroys.
- It never exits on its own after the answer, because unbinding drops an unwritten answer (helpers.ts:1888, 1913-1919).
- Browse's modern `tools/call` path awaits the same promise.

Conformance:
- Lifecycle: the client 'SHOULD NOT send requests other than pings before the server has responded' to `initialize` (clients.md:7), so pings must be answered during the wait.
- An error reply to `initialize` is allowed (clients.md:9).
- JSON-RPC 2.0 reserves -32000 to -32099 for implementation-defined server errors.
- The ping utility's prompt-reply requirement is paraphrased at proposal-server.md:517, but its text is not in the portfolio: NOT-EVIDENCED.
- How each client displays a non-version `initialize` error is unread (clients.md:26-28). Library U10 must settle it for Claude Code before the guide states it.

Release order: `@orkestrel/mcp` 0.0.36 publishes first, then `@orkestrel/browser` re-pins `^0.0.36` (library U1, then U2).
questions: D7 says the pool tracks liveness 'at all times'. Without a scheduled check, which AGENTS.md forbids, an idle browser that hangs is found only when it is next handed work. Do you accept that, or do you want an exception to the no-polling law?

D8 says teardown leaves nothing behind, including after a crash. On POSIX, Chromium spawned by a server that was killed with SIGKILL keeps running until the next `browse` start in the same root reclaims it. Do you accept that, or do you require operating-system containment (an out-of-process reaper)?
At onset, if one browser starts and a configured spare cannot: should `browse` start with fewer browsers and report it (the library and server proposals), or fail startup (the analyst)?

If M2 shows the eager handshake exceeding Codex's 10 s startup default on the target host, do you accept documenting Codex's `startup_timeout_sec` setting rather than answering `initialize` before a browser is warm?

Should a new `browse` start delete the `.profiles/<uuid>` directories that earlier versions left behind, given that a live older server may own them (the server proposal deletes them; the library and analyst proposals leave them)?

strengths: Smallest public surface that meets the case: one ungrouped single-word option `spares`, `ping()` and `endpoint` on `BrowserInterface`, the `BrowserSlot` record in `src/server/types.ts`, three error codes, and qualified constants (proposal-server.md:141-221). It refuses a public `BrowserPool` because no consumer beyond `browse` exists (proposal-server.md:458), which is the minimal-API law read correctly.

Busy and ready are derived from the lease and the ready map, with no stored flag (proposal-server.md:80-81). `#warm` is the only setup path and `#release` the only teardown path (proposal-server.md:23), which matches D8's one place for each.

No polling: liveness comes from `disconnect` and page `crash` events plus a check that work triggers. Every refusal maps to a cited rule (proposal-server.md:501-511): no heartbeat, no reaching `Browser`'s private client, no lazy-launch shim, no fake, no prefixed key, no module-scope slot type, no stored busy flag.
It rejects `@orkestrel/process` `Supervisor` and `@orkestrel/queue` (proposal-server.md:480-481), which matches the user's later ruling.

Attacked and held: holding `transport.start()` does delay every handshake path. `StdioServerTransport.start()` is the only place input is subscribed (mcp/src/server/transports/StdioServerTransport.ts:83-99).
defects: proposal-server.md:227-235 and 353-354: hand-writes pool mechanics that `@orkestrel/pool` already provides and tests. The `#change` wake promise and `#wait` duplicate the waiter queue. `#releasing` plus the aggregated `#release` duplicate the teardown barrier, which in `Pool` waits for in-flight creates, disposes late resources, and aggregates failures as code `cleanup` (pool/src/core/Pool.ts:170-188, 574-587). The `ping` at admit is `PoolOptions.validate` at handoff (Pool.ts:293-305). The proposal never weighs `@orkestrel/pool`. Right: the slot becomes the pool's value, with `#warm` as `create`, `#release` as `destroy`, and the liveness check as `validate`, over the improved pool in the `pool` ruling.

proposal-server.md:217-218: `BROWSER_SERVER_PROFILE_PATTERN` duplicates the `PID-UUID` regex that `parseBrowserLockEntry` already owns (src/server/helpers.ts:47-65). Right: name each profile with `formatBrowserLockEntry` and parse it with `parseBrowserLockEntry` (architecture.md: centralize any pattern repeated twice).

proposal-server.md:76: adds a third `process.kill(pid, 0)` liveness test beside src/server/stores/FileBrowserStore.ts:218-222 and src/server/Browser.ts:1071-1076. Right: one exported helper in `src/server/helpers.ts` that FileBrowserStore routes through as well, as the library proposal specifies (proposal-library.md:78).

proposal-server.md:29-32, 517, 533: holding stdin unread leaves a `ping` unanswered and the end of stdin unobserved during setup. A failure shows only as an exit with a stderr line, and clients.md:28 lists that display as unknown. Right: the `@orkestrel/mcp` handshake hook in the `mcp` ruling.

proposal-server.md:530: after a SIGKILL of the server, the sweep removes profiles but leaves detached POSIX Chromium processes running, so D8's 'leaves nothing behind' fails for processes. Right: record each incarnation's endpoint and close orphans at the next start (graft).

proposal-server.md:227: `#slots: (BrowserSlot | undefined)[]` uses `undefined` to mean the retired state, which is a sentinel carried by absence. Right: drop the retired slot from the pool and keep the strike count as the state the server owns.

strengths: Places mechanism in the library and policy in `browse`: session affinity, loss notes, and `BROWSE_POOL` stay in the server (proposal-library.md:105-114), which matches AGENTS.md 'Mechanism, not product policy'.

Reuses existing helpers: `formatBrowserLockEntry` and `parseBrowserLockEntry`, plus one `probeProcess` helper that FileBrowserStore's pid check routes through (proposal-library.md:76-78). Attacked and held: the helpers exist at src/server/helpers.ts:47-65 and the check at FileBrowserStore.ts:215-222.

Groups the option as `pool: { size }` (proposal-library.md:264) per names.md 'Group options by entity'. Publishes one event per transition with no `status` event (proposal-library.md:384). Derives `started`, `failed`, and `destroyed` instead of storing them (proposal-library.md:308).

Meets D8 after a server kill: a per-life endpoint record lets the next start attach, send `Browser.close`, and then remove the directory (proposal-library.md:77-79). Fixes the false 9222 refusal in the lowest owning layer (proposal-library.md:108-110; quality.md § Ecosystem reuse).

Attacked and held: a `ping` is answered while `initialize` is parked, because `bindServer` runs each inbound message in its own async handler (mcp/src/core/helpers.ts:1868-1907). That handler's request signal aborts when the transport closes, so acceptance U1 (f) is reachable.
defects: proposal-library.md:7, 249-259, 355: `BrowserPool` re-implements `@orkestrel/pool`: the FIFO waiter queue, the exclusive lease with idempotent release, acquire-signal cancellation, the handoff check (`version()` at handoff equals `validate`), 'longest ready' rotation (Pool's `#available` push and shift, Pool.ts:265 and 480), the emitter, and the destroy barrier. It also rejects a generic pool for 'no second real consumer', but a generic pool already exists in the fleet. That breaks AGENTS.md 'ALWAYS inspect … Reuse a primitive whose semantics match' and patterns.md § Declared ecosystem capabilities. Right: improve `@orkestrel/pool` and keep only the browser member in this package.

proposal-library.md:378: refuses `@orkestrel/queue`, `timeout`, `abort`, and `process` by citing AGENTS.md:38. The user's reuse ruling supersedes that ground. Right: rule each package on semantics, as in the `pool` ruling.

proposal-library.md:34: answers a failed setup with `-32603` plus a detailed message and `data`. That contradicts the documented `JSONRPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` contract, 'detail-free on the wire' (mcp/src/core/constants.ts:285-295). Right: `JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR` (-32000, constants.ts:297-305), which the legacy branch already uses for implementation-defined faults (mcp/src/core/MCPLegacy.ts:264-270).

proposal-library.md:236, 252, 287, 522: adds surface no consumer reads. `member(id)` is its own tension 11. `holder` names the only holder a stdio server has. There are 7 error codes, and `BROWSER_POOL_IDLE` names a pool that has not started. Right: keep only what `browse` reads (architecture.md: smallest primitives the capability requires).

proposal-library.md:36, 518: `start()` rejects while the server goes on serving the failure until stdin ends, so the two lifecycles diverge. Right: one setup promise, which the handshake hook awaits and `start()` returns.

strengths: States the limits honestly. 'At all times' liveness cannot be proved without a schedule, and cleanup cannot run in a killed process (proposal-analyst.md:5-6).

Picks the right handshake error: an implementation-defined server error such as -32000, with a stable code in `error.data` (proposal-analyst.md:37). That matches JSON-RPC 2.0 and the package's legacy convention (MCPLegacy.ts:264-270).

Attacked and held: element references alias after a rebuild. `BrowserContext` starts `#reference` at 0 for each context (src/core/BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-349), so a replacement context reissues `e1` and the following references (proposal-analyst.md:113).

Gives the strongest race treatment: one invalidation per generation, and a stale release cannot free a successor's slot (proposal-analyst.md:121-134). It also notes that a failure code must be written into the tool text because the tool layer keeps only the message (proposal-analyst.md:115).
defects: proposal-analyst.md:142, 285: designs its own pool class and lease records without weighing `@orkestrel/pool`. It also hand-writes startup, check, and cleanup deadlines that `@orkestrel/timeout` `createTimeout` provides, and that package is already in the browser's installed graph through `@orkestrel/server`. Right: reuse as in the `pool` ruling.

proposal-analyst.md:192-200: the 8-state `BrowserPoolPhase` folds pool-level `stopping` and `stopped` into a slot union and stores the transient `checking`, against AGENTS.md 'Real domain states only' and 'Derive state', and against D6's small and simple pool. Right: four slot states at most.
proposal-analyst.md:219-224: required `deadline` and `recovery` groups force fixed figures onto every caller, against D5. Right: optional keys with defaults chosen from measurement.

proposal-analyst.md:253: `BrowserLeaseInterface.destroy()` ends a lease, but the fixed lifecycle verb `destroy` means tear down and release resources (names.md § Fixed lifecycle vocabulary), and `@orkestrel/pool` names this act `release`. Right: `release`.

proposal-analyst.md:273: 'contract direction, not checked declarations', with the endpoint, health, timeout, and allocator types left unwritten. That fails the types-first law. Right: declare each type in its owning `types.ts` before its unit.

proposal-analyst.md:28-35, 313-326: adds per-connection initialization state, a write-completion observation, and a closure signal in `@orkestrel/mcp`, plus durable owner records with stronger-than-PID identity and symlink validation. None of these has a consumer in this change (minimal-API law). Right: one handshake hook, plus the endpoint-record sweep.

proposal-analyst.md:117: replacement credits are never replenished, so a second crash on one slot during a long session retires that slot for the owner's lifetime. Right: consecutive failures that a granted lease resets.

grafts: From library U1 (proposal-library.md:425-435): add the `@orkestrel/mcp` `handshake` hook to replace the unread-stdin hold (proposal-server.md:29-32). `browse` passes a handler that awaits the setup promise `start()` began and never starts setup itself.
From analyst (proposal-analyst.md:37): refuse the handshake with `new MCPError(message, JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR, { code })`, which is -32000, not the `-32603` of proposal-library.md:34.

From library (proposal-library.md:76-78): name each incarnation's profile with `formatBrowserLockEntry`, parse it with `parseBrowserLockEntry` (src/server/helpers.ts:47-65), and route FileBrowserStore.ts:215-222 and the sweep through one exported `probeProcess` helper. This replaces `BROWSER_SERVER_PROFILE_PATTERN` (proposal-server.md:217-218) and the server's own `process.kill(pid, 0)` (proposal-server.md:76).

From library (proposal-library.md:77-79; acceptance U5 (f)): write a per-incarnation endpoint record, and at the next start attach to an orphan whose owner pid is dead, send `Browser.close`, and only then remove its profile. This closes proposal-server.md:530 under D8.

From library (proposal-library.md:108-110): skip the 9222 occupancy probe when `cdp.port` is unset (src/server/Browser.ts:320-322, 543-563). Eager start would otherwise move the false refusal to every session start (proposal-server.md:523).

From analyst (proposal-analyst.md:113): add a reference allocator that never reissues a spelling during one server lifetime, threaded through context creation. Each context's `#reference` starts at 0 (src/core/BrowserContext.ts:71, 348-349), so the rebuild in proposal-server.md:57 would alias the dead page's references.

From analyst (proposal-analyst.md:115): write the stable code (`BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH`, `BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`) into the tool-result text, because `ToolManager` keeps only the message (map.md:32).
verdict.pool:
Ruling: improve `@orkestrel/pool` and use it. Keep only the browser member in the browser package, private to the `browse` server: launch, profile, toolset, sweep, and the wiring of liveness events. Lane: codebase laws and reuse.

1. Overlap. All three proposals hand-write what pool/src/core/Pool.ts already provides and tests/src/core/Pool.test.ts tests:
   - the waiter queue and its wake-up;
   - the handoff check, which is `validate` (Pool.ts:293-305);
   - longest-idle rotation, from `#available` push and shift (Pool.ts:265, 480), which is the library's 'longest ready' rule;
   - the exclusive lease with an idempotent release (Pool.ts:217-224, 470-473);
   - abort-safe acquire;
   - the teardown barrier, which waits for in-flight creates, disposes late resources, and aggregates failures as code `cleanup` (Pool.ts:170-188, 574-587).

   Two rules bind here: AGENTS.md 'ALWAYS inspect … Reuse a primitive whose semantics match', and quality.md 'Fix a reusable defect in the lowest package that owns the mechanism'.

2. As is, the pool fails D3 and D7.
   - It creates only inside `acquire` (Pool.ts:272-276), so a replacement would launch on a caller's demand.
   - It never learns that a record died. A dead spare stays in `#available` until the next acquire validates it, and that acquire then pays the launch.
   - This rules out 'use as is'.

3. The gaps are general mechanism, and the engine already holds the internals. `#dispose(record)` already removes a record from the idle, validating, or leased phase (Pool.ts:485-501). A later `release()` of that token is already a no-op (Pool.ts:471). `size` already counts a record until its destroy hook settles. The pool 0.0.14 change is:
   - (a) `PoolOptions.min`: a warm floor, a nonnegative safe integer no greater than `max`.
   - (b) `PoolInterface.start(): Promise<void>`: creates records outside any acquire until owned plus reserved records reach `min`. It resolves when those creates settle and rejects with code `create` on a failure. A failed create is not retried, and the pool never refills on its own. An acquire creates only above the floor, so with `min` equal to `max` no acquire ever launches. Every launch is then the owner's decision (D7), and the crash-loop bound stays with the owner (mechanism, not policy).
   - (c) `create` receives an `evict` function. The creator wires the resource's death event to it. Calling it disposes that record in whatever phase it is in, through `#dispose`, and returns the disposal promise. The owner calls `start()` after that promise settles, so the pool never holds more than `max` live browsers (D6).
   - The change is source-compatible with @orkestrel/worker's zero-argument `create` (worker/src/core/Worker.ts:81-88). Worker can wire a thread's `exit` to `evict`, so a dead thread leaves at once rather than at the next `validate` (worker/src/server/NodeWorker.ts:69-70). That makes worker a second consumer.
   - Refuse a holder identity, because one stdio session holds one token and the token is the lease record. Also refuse event payloads, a member snapshot, and any idle timer: none has a consumer under D6 or D7.

4. The `browse` side is `createPool<BrowserSlot>({ create: #warm, destroy: #release, validate: connected and answering, min: size, max: size })`.
   - The session holds one token across calls.
   - Setup is `pool.start()` plus `acquire()` for the session. The handshake handler awaits that acquire.
   - `#fault` records the loss, counts a strike, and calls `evict`.
   - Strikes and retirement stay private. The private state `#slots`, `#ready`, `#releasing`, and `#change` (proposal-server.md:227-235) goes away.

5. Dependency truth.
   - The browser adds `@orkestrel/pool` at runtime.
   - The pool's `@orkestrel/contract ^0.0.18` pin adds no new version. The browser's install already nests contract 0.0.18 under its direct dependency `@orkestrel/emitter`, and under `router`, `process`, `timeout`, and `abort` (node_modules/@orkestrel/*/node_modules/@orkestrel/contract).
   - The pool uses contract only for value guards (pool/src/core/errors.ts:2, validators.ts:1), so no class identity crosses packages. The pool's release visit re-pins it to ^0.0.19.
   - Release order: pool 0.0.14 and mcp 0.0.36 publish, then the browser declares both.

6. The other packages, ruled on semantics:
   - `@orkestrel/queue`: refuse. It adds `database`, `indexeddb`, and `sqlite` to the runtime graph (capabilities.md, the dependency table), and one lease needs no job queue.
   - `@orkestrel/timeout`: use it only if an aggregate startup deadline is adopted. It is already installed through `@orkestrel/server`; the analyst's hand-written deadlines would duplicate it.
   - `@orkestrel/abort`: not needed. The server's native `AbortController` covers the launch signal.
   - `@orkestrel/process` `Supervisor`: out, per the user. `Browser` keeps its own spawn and group kill.
   - `@orkestrel/emitter`: comes in through the pool.

   Refer the hang-detection choice to the objective lane: a `ping` before each call (server) versus a CDP `timeout` event followed by one check (library), weighed against Codex's 60 s tool budget.
verdict.mcp:
Ruling: change `@orkestrel/mcp` in 0.0.36 with one option, the `handshake` hook from library U1, using the analyst's error code. Change nothing else.

1. Types (src/core/types.ts): `MCPHandshakeHandler = (options: MCPMethodOptions) => Promise<void>`, plus `MCPServerOptions.handshake?`, `MCPServerInterface.handshake`, and `MCPLegacyOptions.handshake?`. `createMCPLegacy` reads `handshake` the same way it reads `identity` (mcp/src/core/factories.ts:88-90).

2. Gating:
   - Legacy `initialize` (MCPLegacy.ts:140-150) and modern `server/discover` await the handler before they answer.
   - `ping` (MCPLegacy.ts:151-152) never awaits it.
   - `bindServer` runs each message in its own handler (mcp/src/core/helpers.ts:1868-1907), so a ping is answered while `initialize` is parked. The request signal aborts when the transport closes, so a client that gives up ends the wait.

3. Refusal:
   - A rejection with an `MCPError` answers under the request id with that error's code and message, and with its `context` as `data`.
   - Any other rejection answers the fixed, detail-free `-32603` and emits `error` once.
   - `browse` rejects with `new MCPError(message, JSONRPC_SERVER_ERROR, { code })`, which is -32000 (constants.ts:297-305). The legacy branch already answers implementation-defined faults with that code (MCPLegacy.ts:264-270).
   - Never use `-32603` for this, because its documented contract is detail-free on the wire (constants.ts:285-295).

4. The handler awaits the setup `start()` began and never starts setup itself. After a failure, `browse` keeps answering the same refusal until stdin ends, then exits 1 with its coded stderr line.

5. Refuse the rest:
   - The analyst's per-connection initialization state, write-completion observation, and closure signal (proposal-analyst.md:28-35): no consumer in this change.
   - A `logging` capability for the onset: the failure travels in the `initialize` answer.

Specification it conforms to:
- MCP lifecycle 2025-11-25 (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle):
  - `initialize` is the first exchange, and the client 'SHOULD NOT send requests other than pings before the server has responded' (clients.md:7), so a ping must be answerable during setup.
  - Before `notifications/initialized` the server sends only pings and logging (clients.md:8), and a parked `initialize` sends nothing.
  - An error reply to `initialize` is allowed (clients.md:9).
  - Every request carries a timeout, and the sender cancels on expiry (clients.md:11). The request signal honors that.
